title: Why Sylhet Gets Rain Like Meghalaya
text:
Sylhet in Bangladesh has a rainfall pattern much like that of Meghalaya in India, home of Cherrapunji and Mawsynram. The reason is their shared geography: the same monsoon winds meet the same line of hills, which triggers a process called orographic precipitation.
Although an international border separates them, the two regions share one weather system. Sylhet’s flat floodplains act as a runway for moist air, and the steep face of the Meghalaya plateau acts as a wall that squeezes the rain out of it.

title: Why Sylhet Gets Rain Like Meghalaya
text:
1. A natural rain machine
From June to September, moisture-laden winds sweep north from the warm Bay of Bengal.

The runway. The winds cross several hundred kilometres of flat Bangladeshi plains with nothing to lift them, so they keep their moisture.
The wall. At the northern edge of the Sylhet division the plain ends suddenly at the southern face of the Meghalaya Plateau (the Khasi and Jaintia Hills), which rises to roughly 1,400 metres near Cherrapunji.
The condensation. The hills force the wind upward. As the air climbs it cools, and cold air holds less water vapour than warm air, so the moisture condenses and falls as heavy rain.

title: Why Sylhet Gets Rain Like Meghalaya
section: 2. Why Sylhet gets a share of the downpour
text:
2. Why Sylhet gets a share of the downpour
The heaviest rain falls on the hills themselves, at Cherrapunji and Mawsynram, among the wettest places on Earth. But Sylhet sits right at the foot of the same wall.

Clouds pile up early. Before the air has climbed the hills, clouds already build over the Sylhet sky. Funnel-shaped valleys push low, heavy clouds over the north and northeast of the division, around places such as Jaflong, Lalakhal and Kanaighat. This makes Sylhet the wettest region of Bangladesh, with typical annual totals of roughly 3,500 to 5,000 mm, depending on the location.
The same seasons. Both regions have dry, pleasant winters, then a wet pre-monsoon spring and a summer when rain can continue for weeks.

title: Why Sylhet Gets Rain Like Meghalaya
text:
The consequence: flash floods
Because the rain comes from the same weather event, the two regions share its effects. When Cherrapunji gets an extreme cloudburst, the water cannot soak into the steep, rocky hills. Within hours, huge volumes run off the Indian slopes and rush down into the low-lying haors (bowl-shaped wetlands) and rivers of Sylhet, such as the Surma and the Kushiyara, causing severe flash floods.

title: Major Tectonic Plates and Subplates
text: The Earth’s lithosphere is broken into 7 or 8 major tectonic plates, depending on how they are classified, and dozens of smaller minor plates, or microplates.

title: Major Tectonic Plates and Subplates
text:
Major plates
These plates cover roughly 94% of the Earth’s surface and carry entire continents and oceans.







Plate
What it covers




Pacific
The largest plate, under most of the Pacific Ocean, ringed by the volcanic “Ring of Fire”.


North American
North America, Greenland, and parts of the Atlantic and Arctic oceans.


Eurasian
The second largest: most of Europe and Asia, and part of the Atlantic.


African
The whole African continent and large parts of the Atlantic and Indian oceans.


Antarctic
Antarctica and the Southern Ocean around it.


Indo-Australian
India, Australia and the oceans between. Often treated as two plates, Indian and Australian, which fused millions of years ago.


South American
South America and the southwestern Atlantic.

title: Major Tectonic Plates and Subplates
text:
Minor plates and subplates
These smaller plates fill the gaps between the major ones. Despite their size, their interactions drive intense earthquake and volcanic activity, especially in the Mediterranean and around the Pacific.

The Americas and the Caribbean

Nazca: a very active oceanic plate subducting under western South America.
Cocos: beneath the Pacific Ocean off Central America.
Juan de Fuca: a small remnant plate subducting under the US Pacific Northwest.
Caribbean: wedged between North and South America, under the Caribbean Sea.



The Mediterranean and the Middle East

Arabian: dominated by the Arabian Peninsula and pushing north into Eurasia.
Anatolian: a microplate under most of Turkey, squeezed westward.
Adriatic (Apulian): a microplate under parts of Italy and the Adriatic Sea.
Aegean Sea: under southern Greece in the eastern Mediterranean.



Asia and the Pacific

Philippine Sea: an oceanic plate responsible for deep ocean trenches.
Scotia: in the South Atlantic and Southern Ocean, between South America and Antarctica.
Amurian: parts of northeast China, the Korean Peninsula and western Japan.
Okhotsk: the Kamchatka Peninsula, the Sea of Okhotsk and northern Japan.

title: Is Turkey Part of the European Plate?
text:
No. Turkey is not on the European tectonic plate.
Geologically, most of Turkey sits on the Anatolian plate. It is part of the wider Eurasian plate system and the Alpide belt. A small southern sliver lies on the Arabian plate.

title: Is Turkey Part of the European Plate?
text:
Tectonic setting
The Anatolian plate is squeezed and pushed westward and southwestward between the larger Eurasian, African and Arabian plates.

title: Is Turkey Part of the European Plate?
text:
Geography vs. tectonics
Only about 3% of Turkey’s land, East Thrace, lies geographically in southeastern Europe. The underlying geology is a different matter. Active fault lines such as the North Anatolian and East Anatolian fault zones belong to the Anatolian/Eurasian collision zone, not to a distinct “European plate”.

title: What Is the East African Rift?
text:
The East African Rift System is a vast, active fracture zone about 6,400 kilometres long, running through eastern Africa. It is like a giant zipper along which the African continent is slowly tearing into two pieces.
Most places where continents pull apart (divergent boundaries) lie deep underwater. The East African Rift is special because it is happening on dry land, giving us a rare view of how new oceans begin. See also how oceans and mountains form.

title: What Is the East African Rift?
text:
How the rift works
Deep below, a broad upwelling of hot mantle rock, often called the African Superplume, heats, stretches and thins the continental crust above it, like a blowtorch under a slab of wax.
As the ground stretches, the African Plate is splitting into two main pieces:

Nubian Plate: the larger piece to the west, holding most of Africa.
Somali Plate: the smaller piece to the east, holding the Horn of Africa and the coast.

They are moving apart very slowly, at roughly 2 to 7 millimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Geologists also recognise a few small microplates in between.

title: What Is the East African Rift?
text:
The landscape it creates
Because the land is pulling apart, the middle blocks drop while the edges rise. This builds some of Earth’s most dramatic scenery:

Rift valleys: the sunken central floor forms the classic Rift Valley, bounded by steep cliffs called fault scarps.
Volcanoes: thin crust lets magma reach the surface. Erta Ale, in Ethiopia, has a long-lived lava lake. Famous peaks such as Mount Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya also stand in the rift region.
Deep lakes: long, narrow depressions on the valley floor fill with water, forming very deep lakes such as Lake Tanganyika and Lake Malawi.

title: What Is the East African Rift?
section: How far along is the split?
text:
How far along is the split?
Studies of the region near Lake Turkana in Kenya report that the crust has thinned to about 13 kilometres, compared with a typical 35 kilometres. Geologists call this stage “necking”, like a pulled candy bar thinning just before it snaps. Parts of the rift are among the best places on Earth to study a continent in this late stage of breaking apart.

title: What Is the East African Rift?
text:
The fate of Africa
There is no need to worry: this takes millions of years. Some projections suggest that in roughly 5 to 10 million years:

the rift valley floor could sink below sea level,
seawater from the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean could flood the basin, and
a new ocean would form, leaving the Somali Plate as a large island continent in the Indian Ocean.

These timescales are estimates and vary between studies.

title: Does Europe Have Its Own Tectonic Plate?
text: No. Geographical Europe does not have its own tectonic plate. Most of the continent sits on the huge Eurasian Plate.

title: Does Europe Have Its Own Tectonic Plate?
text:
The Eurasian Plate
This single lithospheric plate spans all of Europe and most of Asia. The exceptions are the Indian subcontinent, the Arabian Peninsula and easternmost Siberia.
Europe and Asia share one continuous landmass on the same plate, so geologists often treat them as a single unit, Eurasia. The line between the two continents is a cultural, historical and political convention, not a geological boundary.

title: Does Europe Have Its Own Tectonic Plate?
text:
Exceptions at the edges
Not every part of geographical Europe lies on the main body of the Eurasian Plate.

Iceland is split down the middle by the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Its western half rests on the North American Plate.
Southern Europe, such as parts of Italy and Greece, is strongly affected by microplates like the Adriatic Plate, squeezed between Eurasia and the African Plate.

title: Is the Madhupur Fault in Bangladesh Visible to the Naked Eye?
text:
No. You cannot see the Madhupur Fault itself. It is a subsurface structure covered by thick layers of soil. What you can see is its imprint on the landscape: the shapes of the land and rivers that the fault has helped create.
Instead of an open rocky canyon, the fault shows up through sharp contrasts in the land.

title: Is the Madhupur Fault in Bangladesh Visible to the Naked Eye?
text:
1. The red-clay highlands
Travel from the low river plains around Dhaka or Mymensingh towards Gazipur or Tangail and you will notice a change in height and soil colour. The Madhupur Tract is a raised plateau of iron-rich, oxidised red and brown clay. Studies link its uplift to movement along the fault over a very long time.

title: Is the Madhupur Fault in Bangladesh Visible to the Naked Eye?
text:
2. The edge of the tract
The most visible clue is the western edge of the tract, near places such as Ghatail, Madhupur and parts of Mirpur in Dhaka. There the ground steps down, and from the red clay you can look out over the flat, grey alluvial floodplain of the Jamuna-Brahmaputra system. This step looks like a fault scarp. Researchers still debate how much of it was made by the fault, so treat it as a clue, not proof.

title: Is the Madhupur Fault in Bangladesh Visible to the Naked Eye?
text:
3. Diverted rivers
Uplift of this block has also shaped the rivers. The raised tract acted like a wall, and the Old Brahmaputra and Jamuna rivers shifted their channels to flow around it.

title: Is the Madhupur Fault in Bangladesh Visible to the Naked Eye?
section: What is hidden, what is visible
text:
What is hidden, what is visible

Hidden: the fault itself, deep underground, where the blocks of rock grind past each other.
Visible: Sal forests on red soil standing on higher ground, right beside low, flat paddy fields.

title: How Oceans and Mountains Form
text: Oceans and mountains are born from the same engine: the cooling, shifting and recycling of Earth’s tectonic plates. The Earth’s surface area stays fixed, so crust torn apart in one place must be balanced by crust crushed together in another. Oceans open where plates pull apart, and mountains rise where they collide.

title: How Oceans and Mountains Form
text:
Part 1: How the oceans formed
An ocean needs two things: a giant bowl (the ocean basin) and water to fill it.

Rifting (making the bowl). Hot rock rises from deep inside the Earth and weakens the continental crust above it. The crust stretches, cracks and pulls apart, a process called rifting. As the land breaks it sinks into a rift valley, like the modern East African Rift.
Seafloor spreading. As the crust keeps pulling apart, magma wells up into the gap, cools and forms new, dense oceanic crust. Over millions of years the gap widens and pushes the continents apart.
The water. As the early Earth cooled, billions of years ago, volcanoes released huge amounts of water vapour and gas. The vapour condensed into rain that fell for thousands of years and filled the low-lying basins.

title: How Oceans and Mountains Form
section: Part 2: Are oceans and mountains related?
text:
Part 2: Are oceans and mountains related?
Yes. They are two sides of one cycle, known as the Wilson Cycle: oceans open, then close, and mountains form as they do.

The conveyor-belt balance
The Earth cannot grow bigger. If an ocean opens in one place, such as the Atlantic, crust must be destroyed elsewhere. That happens at subduction zones, where dense oceanic crust dives beneath a continent. The collision crumples the land upward and feeds volcanoes, building volcanic mountain ranges like the Andes in South America.


The great crush: when oceans close
Eventually the forces moving the plates change, and an ocean that was widening begins to shrink.

The seafloor is slowly swallowed back into the Earth.
The ocean finally disappears, and the continents on either side collide.
Continental crust is too buoyant to sink, so the two landmasses crumple, fold and thrust upward.

The best example is the Himalayas. Millions of years ago the Tethys Ocean separated India from Asia. As India drifted north, the ocean floor was subducted and vanished. When India finally hit Asia, the squeezed crust rose to form the highest mountains on Earth. Marine fossils, such as ancient seashells, are found high in the Himalayas, even near the summit of Mount Everest, because those rocks were once seafloor.

title: How Oceans and Mountains Form
text:
Oceans vs. mountains









Feature
Driving force
Crust involved
What happens to the crust




Ocean basins
Divergent (pulling apart)
Oceanic: thin, dense, sits low
New crust forms as magma cools.


Mountain ranges
Convergent (pushing together)
Continental: thick, buoyant, sits high
Existing crust is buckled and pushed upward.

title: Tectonic Faults in Simple Terms
text:
A fault is a fracture in the Earth’s crust where blocks of rock on either side have moved past one another. Picture the crust as a cracked hard-boiled eggshell. The pieces, the tectonic plates, constantly crowd, rub and pull away from each other, and the active boundaries where they grind together are faults.
Friction can lock the blocks in place, and stress builds up. When the rock finally breaks or slips, the stored energy is released at once as an earthquake.

title: Tectonic Faults in Simple Terms
text:
A fault is a fracture in the Earth’s crust where blocks of rock on either side have moved past one another. Picture the crust as a cracked hard-boiled eggshell. The pieces, the tectonic plates, constantly crowd, rub and pull away from each other, and the active boundaries where they grind together are faults.
Friction can lock the blocks in place, and stress builds up. When the rock finally breaks or slips, the stored energy is released at once as an earthquake.

title: Tectonic Faults in Simple Terms
text:
The three basic types
Faults are classified by the direction the rocks move.



The three types of faults.



Normal fault: the rocks pull apart (tension), and one block slides down relative to the other.
Reverse (thrust) fault: the rocks push together (compression), forcing one block up and over the other.
Strike-slip fault: the rocks slide horizontally past one another, like cars passing on a highway.

title: Tectonic Faults in Simple Terms
section: Major active fault zones by region
text:
Major active fault zones by region
The Earth has millions of small, local cracks. Geologists track the large, highly active fault systems that pose the greatest seismic hazard.








Region
Notable examples
Main behaviour




North America
San Andreas Fault, Cascadia Subduction Zone, New Madrid Zone
Large horizontal strike-slip movement in California and strong compression in the Pacific Northwest.


South America
Peru-Chile Trench, Boconó Fault
Mostly subduction and reverse faults, where the Pacific floor dives under the continent and lifts the Andes.


Mediterranean and Middle East
North Anatolian Fault, East Anatolian Fault, Dead Sea Transform
A dense network of strike-slip and thrust faults as Africa and Arabia push north into Europe.


East and South Asia
Main Himalayan Thrust, Altyn Tagh Fault, Sagaing Fault
The densest concentration of continental thrust faults on Earth, driven by India pushing into Asia.


Oceania and western Pacific
Alpine Fault (New Zealand), Philippine Fault, Japan Trench
A mix of subduction zones along the “Ring of Fire” and strike-slip faults.


East Africa
East African Rift System
Normal faults, as the continent slowly rips apart, forming deep valleys and lakes.
